how come laguna s2.1 is so good 
Because Laguna S 2.1 is doing something much more interesting than “an 8B model somehow became
frontier-level.” It’s really a 118B-capacity MoE model + enormous training + unusually aggressive
agentic RL + lots of test-time reasoning, while only activating about 8B parameters per token.
The biggest reasons are:
1. 118B total parameters, not 8B total. Laguna S 2.1 has 256 routed experts + one shared expert,
with the router selecting the top 10 routed experts per token. So different tokens can access
different learned sub-networks. You pay roughly 8B-active compute each token, but the model has a
much larger reservoir of specialized knowledge/capacity. 
Think of it roughly as:
That is why comparing it directly to a dense 8B model is misleading.
2. They trained it on an absurd amount of data. Poolside says S 2.1 used exactly the same
pretraining data as XS 2.1. Their earlier Laguna technical report says XS.2/M.1 were trained for
more than 30 trillion tokens, from a roughly 27T-unique-token pool. 
This matters a lot. A model with ~8B active parameters seeing tens of trillions of tokens is extremely
overtrained relative to the old Chinchilla-style regime.
And it wasn't just raw web. Their XS recipe included a very code-heavy mixture: raw code, web,
synthetic/code-text, math, knowledge, academic material, etc. They even trained ~60 small proxy
MoEs to optimize the mixture automatically with their AutoMixer system. 
3. The real secret appears to be post-training, not pretraining. Poolside explicitly says that most of
what separates S 2.1 from the XS models comes from post-training. 
Their pipeline is roughly:
For the preceding Laguna family, Poolside reports roughly 60B tokens of mid-training, followed by
three ~40B-token SFT epochs and then online RL using verifiable rewards. 
That's an enormous amount of post-training compared with the way people often imagine “fine-
tuning.”
4. Their RL tasks are unusually realistic. This is probably the most important piece for why it feels
good when coding.
S 2.1's training corpus includes around 409,000 agentic/non-agentic environments, including
roughly 168,000 software-engineering setups and 83,000 terminal setups. A major source is

5. They reward verification and persistence. This is where Laguna starts behaving noticeably
differently.
Poolside says their objective wasn't merely to make S 2.1 “smarter”; they specifically trained
behaviors such as checking its work, not assuming something succeeded, not stopping after
partial progress, backtracking, and continuing until verification passes. 
Their S 2.1 RL also gave the model:
longer timeouts,
more tokens per turn,
more turns per task,
better sandbox environments,
and the same task executed through multiple agent harnesses. 
So instead of:
attempt → looks plausible → “Done!”
training encourages something closer to:
attempt → run tests → inspect failure → form hypothesis → edit → test → revert if
necessary → try another route → verify → finish.
That loop is enormously valuable for coding.

That's not a tiny bump. The latter is nearly 2.5× the solved-task rate. 
Poolside says they've observed coherent reasoning trajectories lasting hours and hundreds of
thousands of tokens.

Laguna has 118B worth of expert capacity, but spends only ~8B parameters/token; it was exposed to
tens of trillions of tokens; then trained against actual code execution; then taught to persist and verify;
and finally allowed to spend huge amounts of reasoning tokens at inference.
That's why 118B-A8B Laguna can look absurdly better than you'd expect from “8B active.”
And this is particularly relevant to the small-MoE idea we've been discussing: Laguna is a very strong
demonstration that keeping active parameters low while putting enormous effort into data,
verifiable RL, and test-time reasoning can move the performance/compute frontier substantially.
The catch is that Poolside achieved this with 4,096 H200s for S 2.1 pretraining, so the inference
efficiency shouldn't be confused with cheap training. 
Capability = Model Capacity × Data Quality × RL Environment × Verification × Test-Time

At first, S can become surprisingly good. It can learn the teacher's writing style, reasoning patterns,
programming knowledge, explanations, formatting, common facts, math strategies, etc.
But there's a fundamental problem.
The student is learning:
rather than directly learning:
And therefore information that the teacher doesn't generate simply disappears.
The biggest problem: diversity collapse
Imagine reality contains:
very common knowledge       50%
normal knowledge            30%
unusual knowledge           15%
rare/weird edge cases        4%
extremely obscure things     1%
A teacher tends to generate something more like:
very common knowledge       65%
normal knowledge            27%
unusual knowledge            7%
rare/weird edge cases        0.9%
extremely obscure things     0.1%
Train another model on that.
Its outputs could become:
common                       75%
normal                       22%
unusual                       2.8%
rare                          0.2%
Repeat the process enough times and the tails disappear.
That's the classic model-collapse problem identified in recursive synthetic training. Studies find that
replacing real data with successive synthetic generations causes degradation, whereas keeping real data
in the training pool substantially mitigates it. 
So you can end up with a model that sounds extremely polished but has a narrower internal
representation of the world.

"An ~8B-active model, if trained on massive high-quality data and then subjected to
strong verifiable agentic post-training, can enter the neighborhood of models using 20–
50B active parameters."

ESFT is the clearest reason we cannot say “we invented selective MoE expert fine-tuning.” It already freezes
everything except the most task-relevant experts and reports that tuning roughly 5–15% of experts can
match or sometimes exceed full fine-tuning. 
CEFT goes further: it first adapts the router to identify “context-faithful” experts, causally checks them by
masking, and then full-tunes only those selected experts. 
MoE-Sieve is also directly relevant: it profiles routing, selects the most-routed experts per layer, and
attaches LoRA only there. It reports top-25% routed expert LoRA staying approximately competitive with
full LoRA while reducing trainable parameters by 70–73%. 
So selection → sparse adaptation is definitely not new.

Effective supervised-token exposure for every selected expert on selection/train/heldout, not
merely parameter count.
Shared-expert causal sweep. A shared expert is always active and has the same 3,145,728
parameter budget as one routed expert.

outside the causal hierarchy.
Gradient-accessibility measurement on causal/routing candidates.
A new causal × exposure hybrid selector.
Natural-routing vs forced-access training. In forced mode, if the selected expert is absent, it
replaces the lowest-weight top-k expert while keeping that slot's weight. Evaluation always returns
to natural routing.
K=1 vs K=4. K=4 causal selection is a greedy causal coalition using joint interventions, not simply
the four highest individual scores.

what all does the v8 do 
v8 is basically the full cross-capability test of the read-vs-write hypothesis.
It does a lot more than “find high-gradient experts.”
At a high level, for each capability it measures four things for experts:

Frontend is also in the CSV, but not rerun by default because we already studied it deeply.
The pipeline for each capability is:
1. Build clean selection/train/validation/final-test splits.
It uses 50 selection targets, 50 selection controls, 50 train targets, and splits the held-out 50 target +
50 control examples into 25+25 validation and 25+25 untouched final test. It also checks for prompt
leakage and keeps target/control composition stratified.
2. Measure baseline difficulty.
It computes baseline target/control NLL first. This matters because, like you saw with Python,
controls can be much harder than targets. So v8 reports both absolute and relative metrics instead
of pretending raw NLL differences are always comparable.
3. Global routing screen over all 9,984 routed expert positions.
Laguna has 39 sparse layers × 256 experts. For every expert, v8 records supervised target-position
routing statistics such as selection rate and routing mass.
4. Global gradient screen over all 9,984 experts.
One layer at a time, it measures how large the target gradient is for every expert, and also the
control gradient. That produces signals like raw target gradient and target-minus-control gradient
specificity.
5. Hierarchical causal search.
It first ablates all routed experts layer-by-layer to identify the most causally important sparse layers.
Then it searches inside the top causal layers with grouped interventions and progressively narrows
toward individual experts. This is much more defensible than just testing a few hand-picked experts.
6. Greedy causal coalitions.
For K>1, it does not simply take the top individual causal experts. It greedily adds experts based on
their joint intervention effect, so interactions between experts matter.
7. Build a population panel.
It samples 48 experts independently of the scores: roughly one random expert per sparse layer plus
extras. Those 48 are the population sample used for the main statistical analysis.

8. Add sentinels.
It also includes top gradient, gradient-specific, routing, causal candidates, plus known v6/v7 anchors.
These are useful for mechanistic comparisons but are excluded from the primary population
correlations so the statistics are not inflated by preselecting extreme experts.
9. Exact causal measurement on the panel.
For each panel expert it runs fixed-routing ablation and renormalized ablation, measures
target/control damage, causal specificity, relative causal specificity, and bootstrap uncertainty.
10. Precise FP32 gradient geometry.
The global scan is a fast BF16 screening pass. The panel then gets a more precise FP32 measurement
through the exact training path: target gradient norm, control gradient norm, target-control dot
product, cosine, gradient specificity, etc.
11. Actually train every panel expert.
This is the crucial 
 measurement. Every panel expert gets the same target training data, same
trainable parameter budget, same optimizer settings, same number of updates, and is evaluated on
validation. So we can compare what actually happened after training against its
causal/routing/gradient properties beforehand.
12. Compute population 
 statistics.
Across the 48 independently sampled experts, v8 computes Spearman and Kendall correlations
between each pre-training property and later adaptation. It also bootstraps the correlations and
computes partial-rank correlations controlling for routing mass and layer depth.
13. Freeze final selectors from selection data only.
This is important. Validation adaptation does not choose the final winner. Final selectors are chosen
using only selection-derived signals. That prevents “we trained 70 experts and picked whichever
looked best on validation” from contaminating the main selector comparison.
14. Run matched K=1 final confirmation with three seeds.
It compares causal, routing, raw-gradient, and gradient-specific selectors using fresh training runs
and evaluates them on the untouched final test. Same trainable parameter count, same training
data, same optimizer, three training-order seeds.
15. Run K=1/2/4/8 parameter-budget curves.
It asks whether the selector advantage grows or disappears when we allow more experts. It
compares causal coalitions, routing-ranked experts, raw-gradient-ranked experts, and gradient-
specific experts at matched K.
16. Audit the training implementation itself.
Training uses the exact-baseline delta-surgery method we fixed in v6, so the model is numerically
identical before training. After training, v8 also physically writes the trained expert slices back into
Laguna's fused BF16 expert tensors and evaluates through the native kernel as a secondary
deployment check.
17. Protect the frozen base.
After every training arm it restores and checks the original base expert tensors so one run cannot
contaminate the next.
18. Checkpoint everything.

Because our results suggest post-training has a location-selection problem, not just an optimizer
problem.
Right now, PEFT methods usually ask something like: “which parameterization should I train?”—LoRA
ranks, adapters, selected layers, expert modules, etc. What our Laguna work is asking is different:
That difference is what could matter across all of those areas.
For PEFT, instead of putting LoRA modules across dozens of layers or training every expert that happens
to route the task, you could first run a cheap writeability scan, choose perhaps K=1, 4, or 8 experts, and
train only those. One Laguna routed expert is about 3.15M parameters, so K=4 is only about 12.6M
trainable parameters inside a ~33B model. Yet in Python, a single gradient-selected expert gave about
+0.366 target improvement, versus only about +0.061 for the routing-selected expert at exactly the
same one-expert budget. So the advantage is not “more trainable parameters”; it's better placement of
the same training budget.

so what all the notebook does and what all it tests
The v9 notebook is basically the direct practical test of everything we learned in v6–v8.
Its central question is:
Instead of only showing that gradient accessibility correlates with expert plasticity, v9 puts writeability
selection head-to-head against conventional PEFT on a real benchmark.
It uses GSM8K as the target capability and MBPP as an unrelated coding control. GSM8K provides 32
selection examples, 256 actual post-training examples, 64 validation examples, and 128 untouched
official test examples. MBPP contributes 32 selection controls, 64 validation controls, and 128 untouched
final controls.
The complete experiment does the following:
1. Freezes a reproducible benchmark snapshot. It downloads pinned GSM8K and MBPP revisions,
deterministically chooses the rows, checks for leakage and duplicates, saves the exact dataset
snapshot locally, and SHA256-fingerprints it.
2. Loads Laguna XS.2 directly in BF16 on the RTX PRO 6000 and validates the expected 40-layer / 39-
MoE-layer architecture. It uses the same corrected Laguna checkpoint conversion and exact teacher-
forcing boundary:
3. Measures baseline GSM8K and MBPP behavior before changing anything. That gives us the
denominator for target improvement and collateral damage.
4. Searches Laguna for expert write locations using selection data only. It performs global routing
over all 9,984 routed expert positions, global expert-gradient scanning, hierarchical fixed-routing
causal search, greedy causal coalition construction, and precise FP32 gradient reranking. From that it
freezes four principled expert rankings—routing, causal, raw gradient, and gradient-specific—plus a
random-expert baseline.
